chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 151 to 160, Ammuvanar's neythal decade of the white heron: every poem opens on the simple-gaited stork that went to see what it took for the white heron's chick, and turns to the lord of the shore, with the woman refusing a melted heart, the friend reporting that he will marry, the woman complaining of the town's lies and of a sedge doll borne to a man who leaves with the tide, and the friend demanding back her beauty and begging him to embrace her.

151.reading: The woman says that for the lord of the shore, where the neythal that opened like an eye when the simple-gaited stork trod on it, going to see what it took for the white heron's chick, keeps on breathing out its honey scent, she will not give in to the heart that has melted.
151.nuance: The decade's refrain turns on செத்தென, which can mean 'taking it for' or 'having died': either the stork mistook something for the heron's chick or went to see a chick that had died; this poem's reading does not depend on which. The flower that blooms under the foot that crushes it is the poem's whole argument: the hurt itself made her open to him, which is why she must refuse with her will what her heart has granted.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flower and the lord of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the neythal flower opened under the stork's foot

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the first-person refusal நேர்கல் லேனே, set against a heart that has already melted (நெக்க நெஞ்சம்), is a woman holding out against her own yielding, so the occasion is read as oodal; whether she answers the friend or a go-between cannot be fixed

ullurai.tenor: the hero who has hurt her and the woman who still softens toward him

pairs.situation: the flower opens at the very tread that crushes it, as she softens at his wrong
its scent will not stop, as her love goes on unasked
the treader is a simple, blundering bird, as the hero's wrong is careless rather than meant

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses a flower and a bird of her own shore, things she knows (porul 7.26)

152.reading: Where the simple-gaited stork cries out helplessly in the lonely seaside grove, they say the lord of the shore will marry her; he seems a man of virtue, and that too is grace.
152.nuance: போலும் here is the particle of seeming, not a comparison: the speaker will believe he is virtuous only when the marriage happens. The helpless cry of the stork in the lonely grove is the grief the news is meant to end, set beside it without comment.

thinai_evidence.note: the seaside grove and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the news reported with என்ப (they say) and weighed as grace reads as the friend telling the woman, in the lonely stage of secret love, that marriage is coming

153.reading: Will the intimacy of the lord of the shore, whose heaped sand gets a covering from the down shed by the shaking stork, seek out the girl of the fine long hair?
153.nuance: A near miss for ullurai: the shore gains its covering from feathers the bird drops without meaning to, and one may hear the lord's affection as just as idle a gift, but only one pair maps, so condition 3 fails. The sense of போர்வின் பெறூஉம் is read as the sand getting a covering; the line is hard.

thinai_evidence.note: the heaped sand of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the doubting question about his கேண்மை reads as the friend's, in secret love before marriage

154.reading: With the lord of the shore where the simple-gaited stork roosts in the seaside grove, what can I do? this town tells lies.
154.nuance: Read as gossip: the town says what is not so, and she can neither stop it nor make it true. Another reading takes பொய்க்கும் as 'will prove false' of the man; the line will bear both.

thinai_evidence.note: the seaside grove and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the first-person யானெவன் செய்கோ and the complaint against the town read as the woman, in secret love, troubled by the gossip

155.reading: For the lord of the shore who goes away with the tide, where neythal flowers crushed as the stork flutters float down the backwater, I have borne a doll of green sedge, the woman says.
155.nuance: The sedge doll is a girl's toy, so to say she has 'borne' one to him is to say their union has left her a child still, with no issue and no standing. A near miss for ullurai (the flowers the stork crushes and the tide carries off, the man who comes and goes with it) fails condition 3 on a second clear pair.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal of the backwater and the tide

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the first-person ஈன்றனென் யானே is the woman's; the bitter claim to have borne only a sedge doll reads as secret love that has given her nothing a mother could show

156.reading: The lord of the shore, where the red-flecked down that the fluttering stork has shed spreads over the clear backwater, is to me a lover and to my mother someone else.
156.nuance: One man, two names in one house: the poem states in a line the whole difficulty of secret love before it is disclosed, and so the need for marriage, without asking for it.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the first-person எனக்கோ against அனைக்கோ is the woman's, in secret love that the mother does not know

157.reading: Where the stork stays through the morning and roosts at evening by the clear sea, our dear one did not come with the lord of the shore; he came by himself.
157.nuance: The bird that is there from morning to evening is set against a lord who is not, which favours the reading in which the man stays away and someone dear comes alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the clear sea and its lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the speaker and the stage cannot be fixed: if எம் காதலோன் is the woman's lover, she reports that he came in person; if it is her son, as the phrase can mean, the wife says the boy came home without his father

158.reading: The friend says that the lord of the cool shore, where the stork wheels about with its mate on the great grove-side shore, is the cause of the sorrow we see on her friend's lovely dark body.
158.nuance: கண்டிக்கும் is read as the decade-neighbour's refrain கண்டிகும், 'we saw'.

thinai_evidence.note: the seaside grove and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; எம் தோழியது துயரே is the friend speaking of the woman; the hearer is not named, and may be the man in hearing

iraicchi.act: the stork goes about the shore together with its mate
iraicchi.sense: even the stork keeps its mate beside it, while the lord leaves her to a sorrow that shows on her body

159.reading: The friend tells the lord of the cold-water shore, where the stork rests while hunger eats at it, that she is not begging anything of him: let him give back the beauty he took from her and go.
159.nuance: 'I am not begging' is the edge of the line: what she asks is not a gift but a return, so his refusal would be theft, not stinginess. The stork that waits hungry is a mood here, not an act the lovers share, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold water of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the address சேர்ப்ப and the demand for her friend's beauty read as the friend pressing the lover toward marriage

160.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore that on top of her pain the sickness grows, and grieving far more than before she is badly bewildered: embrace her, lord.
160.nuance: நொந்ததன் தலையும் may also be heard of the stork, which went to see a chick taken for dead and now grieves on top of grief, so the refrain's bird is the woman's double; the friend does not draw the match.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai only, no thurai; the vocatives துறைவ and பெரும and the plea to embrace her are the friend's to the lover

links.note: Both are the woman speaking of her heart against the man in oodal: the couplet says the heart's anger is false because it yields at the sight of him; Ainkurunuru 151 grants that the heart has already melted and refuses all the same.
links.teaches: The couplet treats a heart that yields as proof the quarrel was never real, while the poem keeps the refusal standing after the heart has gone over, so the Sangam woman's oodal is a decision of will against her own feeling rather than a mood that the man's presence dissolves.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 154's woman can only call the town a liar and ask what she can do; in Kuruntokai 34 the friend says the town would not believe their denials (மறுப்பத் தேறலர்) and is silenced only by the sweet news that the lord will marry her.
links.teaches: Read together they show that in the neythal love story gossip cannot be ended by calling it false, since the town does not believe denials, and the only cure the poets allow is marriage, which turns the lying town into one that rejoices.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 159's friend demands that the lord give back her friend's beauty and go, insisting she is not begging; Kuruntokai 349's heroine refuses her friend's proposal to take back their beauty, saying that asking for it back is like demanding the return of what was given to those who begged, and worse than losing life.
links.teaches: On a defensible reading the two make incompatible claims about the demand 'give back her beauty', a just reclaiming of what was taken or a shameful asking-back of a gift, which shows the formula belonged to the friend's voice and that the heroine could reject it as beneath her.

links.note: Both are Ammuvanar's and end on the same demand, தந்தனை சென்மோ ... நலனே and நலம் தந்து சென்மே; Natrinai 395's colophon says the friend uses it to press the lover to marry.
links.teaches: The same poet's colophoned use of the formula supplies the occasion that this decade's colophons leave out, so 159's demand for the beauty back can be read as a push to marriage (வரைவு கடாயது) rather than a farewell.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives the thinai only, no thurai; every speaker is inferred from the poem and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
The decade title as printed reads வெள்ளங் குருகுப் பத்து, while the refrain in every poem reads வெள்ளாங் குருகின்; the title appears to have lost the long vowel.
156 line 4 reads தெள்கழிப், where the sandhi of தெள் + கழி would give தெண்கழி or தெட்கழி; the form looks unassimilated.
158 line 4 reads கண்டிக்கும், where the sense 'we saw' wants கண்டிகும், as in the refrain of decade 13; possibly a misprint.
157 lines 4 and 5 can be parsed two ways (எம் காதலோன் as the lover or as the son), and the sense of the poem changes with it.
